subject: Mathematics
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 8 periods = 320 minutes
Total: 8 periods · 5h 20min

periods.activity_title: Can 1/3 Be Bigger Than 1/2? Grid Shading Discovery

tasks_in_class.description: Shade 1/8 of Grid A in red, 1/6 of Grid B in blue, 1/12 of Grid C in yellow; mark 1/3 in any grid.

time_bands.activity: Open with the puzzle: can 1/3 of one chocolate be bigger than 1/2 of another? Invite a quick show of hands — who thinks yes, who thinks no — then hold the answer and let curiosity carry the unit forward.

Playing with a Grid, p.17 ("shade 1/8 red, 1/6 blue, 1/12 yellow...."). Distribute grid sheets. Students shade each fraction, then mark 1/3 on a grid of their choice. Pairs compare their shaded regions and discuss which coloured region looks largest and why.

Whole-class share-out: display two grids of different sizes. Ask — if we shade 1/3 of this small grid and 1/3 of that large grid, which shaded piece is bigger? Draw out the idea that a fraction names a part of its own whole, so the same fraction name can represent different amounts when the wholes differ.

periods.teacher_notes: A frequent slip at this stage is treating fraction symbols as fixed amounts independent of the whole — students may insist 1/3 is always smaller than 1/2. Ground each comparison in the specific grid being used, and return to the opening puzzle to confirm that 1/3 of a large chocolate can exceed 1/2 of a small one. Having physical grid sheets for every student, rather than one shared display, gives each child a concrete referent.
materials: Printed grid sheets (Grid A 8-cell, Grid B 6-cell, Grid C 12-cell)
Red, blue, and yellow crayons or coloured pencils

section_titles: Fun with Fraction Kit — Equivalent Fractions
periods.activity_title: Fitting Pieces: Discovering Equivalent Fractions With the Kit

tasks_in_class.description: In groups of 3–4, find different ways to make a whole with different fraction pieces; write equivalent fractions for 1/3, 1/4, 1/5, 1/6.
Using kit or shading, find how many 1/6s make 1/3.
Using kit or shading, find how many 1/12s make 1/2, 1/3, 1/4, and 1/6.

time_bands.activity: Introduce the fraction kit: show a 1/2 piece and two 1/4 pieces. Lay the two 1/4 pieces on the 1/2 piece so students see they match exactly. Ask: what does that tell us about 1/2 and 2/4?

Let Us Do Q1, p.19 ("find different ways to make a whole with fraction pieces...."). Groups of 3–4 assemble wholes using different-sized pieces, then record each combination as an equivalent fraction statement for 1/3, 1/4, 1/5, and 1/6.

Let Us Do Q2A, p.19 ("find how many 1/6s make 1/3") and Let Us Do Q2C(a)–(d), p.19 ("find how many 1/12s make 1/2, 1/3, 1/4, and 1/6"). Students lay smaller pieces onto larger pieces to count and record. Additional practice: Let Us Do Q2B(a)–(b), p.19.
Quick class debrief: write two equivalences on the board (e.g. 1/3 = 2/6, 1/4 = 3/12). Ask students to say in one sentence what they notice — same amount, different names.

periods.teacher_notes: Equivalence through fitting is the conceptual anchor here — students are discovering that different fraction names can describe identical regions, not yet applying a multiplication rule. A common error is writing the count of pieces as the numerator without keeping the denominator tied to the whole (e.g. writing '2' instead of '2/6'); encourage students to write the full fraction each time. Let Us Do Q7, p.20 (mixed combinations) is noted as additional practice for groups that finish early.
materials: Fraction kit sets (one per group of 3–4)

section_titles: Fun with Fraction Kit — Equivalent Fractions
periods.activity_title: From Fitting Pieces to the Multiply Rule

tasks_in_class.description: Using fraction kit, make a whole using only 1/6 and 1/12 pieces; using 1/12, 1/4, and 1/2 pieces; any five same-size pieces; any seven pieces.
Fill in blanks with equivalent fractions for 1/7, 2/3, 3/4, 3/5 (more than one answer possible).
Put a tick against pairs that are equivalent: 2/3 & 3/4; 3/5 & 6/10; 4/12 & 2/6; 6/9 & 1/3.
Fill boxes to make equivalent fractions: 2/5 = ?/10; 3/4 = ?/16; 4/7 = 8/?; 5/9 = ?/25.

time_bands.activity: Let Us Do Q3, p.20 ("make a whole using only 1/6 and 1/12 pieces...."). Students build four different combinations, then write each as a fraction sentence. Bridge to the pictorial: if Sameer shades 1/3 of a shape and then cuts it into smaller equal parts, the shaded area does not change — it just gets a new name.

Let Us Do Q1, p.22 ("fill blanks with equivalent fractions for 1/7, 2/3, 3/4, 3/5...."). Students draw division lines on printed figures or notebook shapes to generate the chains, noticing that multiplying both parts by the same number works.

Let Us Do Q2, p.22 ("tick equivalent pairs: 2/3 & 3/4; 3/5 & 6/10; 4/12 & 2/6; 6/9 & 1/3"). Students apply the pattern they have just observed, checking each pair by reasoning about the multiply relationship.
Let Us Do Q3, p.22 ("fill boxes: 2/5 = ?/10; 3/4 = ?/16; 4/7 = 8/?; 5/9 = ?/25"). Students work individually, then one student per question explains the reasoning aloud.

periods.teacher_notes: The pivot from kit to symbolic happens in this unit: the multiply pattern should feel discovered, not handed down. A common error is multiplying only the numerator or only the denominator; press students to explain what they did to both numbers. The fraction kit section's open-combination task (Q3, p.20) is a strong warm-up because it revisits hands-on equivalence just before the pictorial bridge.
materials: Printed figure sheets for Q1 p.22 (or plain notebooks)

periods.activity_title: Same Pieces, Same Slices: Two Comparison Strategies

tasks_in_class.description: Compare fractions with same denominator using < and >: 1/4 & 3/4; 3/5 & 4/5; 5/7 & 2/7; 7/8 & 3/8; 5/10 & 6/10; 2/6 & 1/6.
Compare fractions with same numerator using < and >: 3/8 & 3/7; 4/9 & 4/10; 2/7 & 2/5; 5/7 & 5/6; 6/9 & 6/10; 7/9 & 7/11.

time_bands.activity: Read the chikki-sharing story (p.22–23): Sevi ate 1/3, Shami ate 2/3 of the same chikki. Draw two equal strips on the board, shade 1 out of 3 and 2 out of 3. Ask: which is more, and how do you know? Draw out the idea — same-size pieces, so count the pieces.
Let Us Do Q1, p.23 ("compare same-denominator pairs with < and >...."). Students write each pair and insert the correct symbol, explaining the reasoning in one phrase beside each answer.

Introduce the paratha contrast (p.23): 4/6 vs 4/5 — same number of pieces, but which piece is bigger? Use fraction-kit circles divided into fifths and sixths so students see that one sixth is wider than one fifth. Ask: when numerators match, what does the denominator tell us?

Let Us Do Q1 (same-numerator section), p.23 ("compare same-numerator pairs: 3/8 & 3/7; 4/9 & 4/10...."). Students work through all six pairs, then a brief pair-share: name which strategy they used for each comparison and why.

periods.teacher_notes: The two strategies taught here run in opposite directions — bigger numerator wins (same denominator) versus bigger denominator loses (same numerator) — and students frequently confuse them. Encourage students to state the rule they are using before writing each symbol. Fraction-kit circles are valuable for the same-numerator discussion because the size difference between a fifth-slice and a sixth-slice is visible before any symbol is introduced.

periods.activity_title: Beyond One Whole: Parathas, Improper Fractions, and the Number Line

tasks_in_class.description: Use parathas and number lines in notebook to show 2/3 & 5/3; 3/4 & 5/4; 4/8 & 9/8.
Circle fractions greater than 1 from the given set; discuss reasoning in class.

time_bands.activity: Introduce Raman's family sharing parathas (p.26–27). Each paratha is cut into halves; five halves are taken — draw five half-circles on the board. Count them: 1/2, 2/2, 3/2, 4/2, 5/2. Ask: does 5/2 fit on the same number line as 1/2? Where does it land?

Let Us Do Q1, p.28 ("use parathas and number lines to show 2/3 & 5/3; 3/4 & 5/4; 4/8 & 9/8...."). Students draw paratha diagrams for each pair, then mark both fractions on a number line drawn in their notebooks, labelling whole-number points.

Let Us Do Q2, p.28 ("circle fractions greater than 1; discuss reasoning...."). Students circle fractions where numerator exceeds denominator and articulate the reasoning — the whole has been exceeded. Class discussion draws out the generalisation: if the numerator is larger than the denominator, the fraction is greater than 1.

periods.teacher_notes: Students sometimes think 'fraction' always means 'less than one whole' — the paratha images are a concrete corrective. Encourage students to say the fraction as a count of unit pieces ('five halves') before placing it on the number line. A common error is misreading 9/8 as 'nearly one' without noticing it crosses 1; verifying by counting unit jumps on the number line addresses this.
materials: Paratha cut-out cards or drawn paratha diagrams
Rulers for number lines in notebooks

periods.activity_title: Is It More or Less Than One Whole? The Benchmark 1 Strategy

time_bands.activity: Write 7/8 and 8/6 on the board. Ask: without finding a common denominator, can we say which is bigger? Introduce the benchmark 1 idea: if the numerator is smaller than the denominator, the fraction is below 1; if larger, it is above 1. One fraction is below 1, the other is above — so the comparison is settled immediately.

Let Us Do Q1, p.29 ("compare pairs using 1 as reference: 8/7 & 9/15; 13/20 & 17/15...."). Students first classify each fraction as above or below 1 (or equal to 1), then use that classification to write the comparison symbol. Work through all six pairs.

Pair-share and class check: for each pair, one student names the classification of each fraction, another states the result. Focus the debrief on the pair 6/6 & 19/12 — both are ≥ 1, so a second step is needed. Discuss how the benchmark strategy narrows the problem even when it does not fully resolve it.

periods.teacher_notes: Students who have built understanding from the fractions-greater-than-1 concept will recognise immediately when a fraction exceeds the whole. Watch for the pair 6/6 & 19/12 — both exceed or equal 1, so this pair requires additional reasoning; use it as a productive challenge rather than marking it wrong in passing. The benchmark-1 strategy is a shortcut that complements, rather than replaces, the earlier same-denominator and same-numerator strategies.

periods.activity_title: Above or Below Half? The Benchmark 1/2 Strategy

tasks_in_class.description: Circle fractions equal to 1/2 from the given set: 2/4, 3/5, 5/7, 7/14, 5/10, 8/16, 5/9, 6/12, 10/20, 6/8.
If an ant is 1/4 cm long, find total length of 16 such ants in a line using the number line.

time_bands.activity: Write 3/6 on the board and ask: is this exactly half? How do you know? Then write 4/8 — same question. Establish that a fraction equals 1/2 when the numerator is exactly half the denominator. Let Us Do Q1, p.30 ("circle fractions equal to 1/2: 2/4, 3/5, 5/7, 7/14....") — students work quickly and compare answers. Additional practice: Let Us Do Q2, p.30 (circle fractions less than half).

Let Us Do Q3, p.31 ("compare 8 fraction pairs using 1/2 as reference...."). Students classify each fraction as above, below, or equal to 1/2, then use those positions to write the comparison. Pair-share after every two pairs.

Try This, p.31 ("if an ant is 1/4 cm, find total length of 16 ants using the number line"). Students draw a number line, mark 1/4 intervals, and count 16 jumps, recording the result as a fraction and as a whole or mixed number.

periods.teacher_notes: A common error is comparing numerators directly without checking which benchmark applies — students write 2/9 > 4/7 because 4 > 2 without noticing that 2/9 is well below 1/2 while 4/7 is above it. Reinforce the two-step process: locate each fraction relative to 1/2 first, then compare positions. The ant problem is a useful check — students who can count 16 quarter-jumps and record 16/4 = 4 cm have internalised the number-line model for fractions greater than 1.

section_titles: Fun with Fraction Kit — Equivalent Fractions
periods.activity_title: The Fraction Challenge: Choose Your Strategy, Justify Your Answer

time_bands.activity: Warm-up rapid-fire round: the teacher calls out a fraction pair and students hold up a card or slate showing < , > , or =. Use pairs that span all four comparison strategies — same denominator, same numerator, benchmark 1, benchmark 1/2. No discussion yet; pace is quick and energising.

Strategy sorting task: give each pair of students a set of twelve comparison cards (prepared by teacher: pairs such as 3/5 & 6/10; 5/8 & 5/9; 7/6 & 4/5; 9/17 & 4/7; 2/5 = ?/10). Students sort the cards into four labelled columns — Same Denominator, Same Numerator, Benchmark 1, Benchmark 1/2 — then complete the comparison or missing value for each card. Equivalent-fraction cards (e.g. 2/5 = ?/10) belong in a fifth column labelled Equivalent Fractions.

Groups of three share one card from each column and explain their strategy to the class. The teacher asks: 'Which strategy did you choose and why?' and 'Could you have used a different strategy here?' This surfaces the idea that some pairs yield to more than one method.

Exit reflection: each student writes one sentence naming the strategy they find most powerful and one sentence naming the strategy that surprised them most. Collect or share aloud. Close by returning to the opening puzzle from the fractions-of-different-wholes section: a fraction is always a fraction of a particular whole — that idea underpins every comparison strategy practised across the chapter.

periods.teacher_notes: This synthesis unit draws on the full range of ideas built across the chapter — fractions of different wholes, equivalence through fitting and multiplication, and four comparison strategies. The strategy-sorting task is designed to surface metacognitive awareness: students must decide which tool applies before applying it, mirroring the adjunct competency of choosing an appropriate method. Watch for students who default to the same-denominator strategy for every pair by computing equivalent fractions unnecessarily; the sorting task reveals this habit and gives a concrete moment to discuss efficiency.
materials: Pre-cut comparison-card sets (12 cards per pair, including both comparison pairs and equivalent-fraction fill-in cards)
Slate or mini whiteboards for warm-up (optional)

items.prompt: Here are two rectangles. Rectangle P has 8 equal parts. Rectangle Q has 12 equal parts. Shade 1/8 of Rectangle P and 1/12 of Rectangle Q. Which shaded part is bigger? Write one sentence to explain your answer.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 1/8 of Rectangle P is bigger than 1/12 of Rectangle Q, because Rectangle P's parts are larger — even though both fractions are one part of their own whole.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compare the size of one equal part in each rectangle by looking at how many equal parts the whole is divided into.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student cut paper strips into 8 and 12 parts and place them side by side; stretch: ask what fraction of Rectangle Q would equal 1/8 of Rectangle P.

exercise.description: Shade 1/8 of Grid A in red, 1/6 of Grid B in blue, 1/12 of Grid C in yellow; mark 1/3 in any grid.

items.section_title: Fun with Fraction Kit — Equivalent Fractions
items.prompt: Riya has fraction pieces. She places two 1/6 pieces on top of a 1/3 piece and finds they fit exactly. Write the equivalent fraction this shows. Now try: how many 1/6 pieces would cover a 2/3 piece? Write your answer and explain in one sentence.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Two 1/6 pieces cover 1/3, showing 1/3 = 2/6. Four 1/6 pieces would cover 2/3, because 2/3 is twice as large as 1/3, so you need twice as many 1/6 pieces.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Lay smaller fraction pieces onto the larger piece and count how many fit to find the equivalent fraction.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student draw and shade two equal strips and divide one into sixths to count; stretch: find how many 1/12 pieces cover 2/3.

exercise.description: In groups of 3–4, find different ways to make a whole with different fraction pieces; write equivalent fractions for 1/3, 1/4, 1/5, 1/6.

items.section_title: Fun with Fraction Kit — Equivalent Fractions
items.prompt: Using fraction pieces, Priya finds that several 1/12 pieces cover exactly 1/4. How many 1/12 pieces does she need?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Count how many 1/12 pieces fit onto a 1/4 piece by recognising that 3 × (1/12) = 3/12 = 1/4.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student may be thinking of 1/6 pieces rather than 1/12 pieces, confusing two different equivalent-fraction relationships.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student may be applying the denominator directly (thinking '4 twelfths make one fourth') without recognising that 1/4 is larger than 1/12.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student may be recalling how many 1/12s make 1/2, applying a remembered fact to the wrong target fraction.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student draw a strip divided into 12 equal parts and shade 1/4 of it to count the shaded parts; stretch: find how many 1/12 pieces make 3/4.

exercise.description: Using kit or shading, find how many 1/12s make 1/2, 1/3, 1/4, and 1/6.

items.prompt: Draw a number line from 0 to 2. Mark the points 3/4 and 5/4 on it. Which fraction is greater than 1? How can you tell by looking at the number line?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 5/4 is greater than 1. On the number line, 5/4 lands to the right of 1 because it takes 5 quarter-jumps from 0, which goes past the 4/4 = 1 mark.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Count unit-fraction jumps from 0 on the number line and check whether the fraction lands before or after the whole-number mark 1.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student mark each quarter-jump (1/4, 2/4, 3/4, 4/4, 5/4) one by one; stretch: mark 9/4 on the same number line and name the mixed number it equals.

exercise.description: Use parathas and number lines in notebook to show 2/3 & 5/3; 3/4 & 5/4; 4/8 & 9/8.

items.prompt: Which of these pairs of fractions are equivalent?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 3/5 and 6/10, because multiplying both 3 and 5 by 2 gives 6 and 10.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Check whether the numerator and denominator of one fraction are obtained by multiplying those of the other by the same number.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student may be confusing closeness of numerators/denominators with equivalence, not applying the multiply-both-by-same-number check.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student may have divided only the numerator (6 ÷ 6 = 1) without checking the denominator (9 ÷ 6 is not a whole number), revealing a partial-division error.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student may be guessing based on consecutive numbers rather than checking the multiplicative relationship.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student draw two equal strips and divide them differently to compare shaded regions; stretch: write two more equivalent pairs of their own and explain why they are equivalent.

exercise.description: Put a tick against pairs that are equivalent: 2/3 & 3/4; 3/5 & 6/10; 4/12 & 2/6; 6/9 & 1/3.

items.prompt: Anu ate 3/7 of a roti and Ben ate 3/5 of the same-sized roti. Who ate more? Write one sentence explaining why, without drawing a picture.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Ben ate more. When the numerators are the same, the fraction with the smaller denominator is larger because each piece is bigger — fifths are bigger than sevenths.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: When numerators are equal, compare denominators: the smaller denominator means larger pieces, so that fraction is greater.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student draw two equal strips divided into 5 and 7 parts respectively and shade 3 of each; stretch: ask the student to write a similar problem using 4/9 and 4/11 and explain the answer.

exercise.description: Compare fractions with same numerator using < and >: 3/8 & 3/7; 4/9 & 4/10; 2/7 & 2/5; 5/7 & 5/6; 6/9 & 6/10; 7/9 & 7/11.

items.prompt: Which of the following fractions is greater than 1?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 11/10 is greater than 1 because its numerator (11) is larger than its denominator (10).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: A fraction is greater than 1 when its numerator is larger than its denominator.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student may be selecting a fraction whose numerator and denominator look large without comparing them to each other.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student may associate fractions with 'nearly 1' and pick the one closest to 1 without recognising that 'greater than 1' requires the numerator to exceed the denominator.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student may be making a random selection, suggesting the benchmark concept has not yet been internalised.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student write the fraction as repeated unit-fraction additions and count whether the total passes 1; stretch: list three fractions greater than 1 and three less than 1 and explain the pattern.

exercise.description: Circle fractions greater than 1 from the given set; discuss reasoning in class.

items.prompt: Compare 9/7 and 11/15. Write which is greater and explain using the benchmark 1.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 9/7 is greater. 9/7 is greater than 1 because 9 > 7. 11/15 is less than 1 because 11 < 15. A fraction greater than 1 is always greater than a fraction less than 1.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Check whether each fraction's numerator is greater than, less than, or equal to its denominator to place it relative to 1, then compare positions.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student draw a number line and mark 1, then decide on which side each fraction falls; stretch: find a pair where both fractions exceed 1 and explain how to compare them.

items.prompt: Which of the following fractions is equal to 1/2?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: A fraction equals 1/2 when its numerator is exactly half its denominator.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student may be confusing 'more than half' (3/5 > 1/2) with 'equal to half', not checking the doubling relationship.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student may be choosing a fraction close to 1/2 without verifying that 5 is not exactly half of 9.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student may recognise 4/6 as equivalent to 2/3 but mistake it for 1/2 by focusing on even numerator and denominator rather than the halving relationship.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student fold a paper strip and compare the folded half to a coloured part; stretch: write three more fractions equal to 1/2 and explain the pattern.

exercise.description: Circle fractions equal to 1/2 from the given set: 2/4, 3/5, 5/7, 7/14, 5/10, 8/16, 5/9, 6/12, 10/20, 6/8.

items.prompt: Compare 5/9 and 4/7. Use 1/2 as your benchmark. Write which is greater and explain your reasoning in two sentences.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 4/7 is greater. 5/9 is less than 1/2 because 5 is less than half of 9 (half of 9 is 4.5). 4/7 is more than 1/2 because 4 is more than half of 7 (half of 7 is 3.5). A fraction above 1/2 is always greater than a fraction below 1/2.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compare each fraction's numerator to half its denominator: if the numerator is greater, the fraction exceeds 1/2; if less, it falls below.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student use a number line marked with 0, 1/2, and 1 and place both fractions approximately; stretch: find a pair where both fractions are above 1/2 and explain how to compare them then.

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Find the factor that takes the denominator from 3 to 12, then multiply the numerator by the same factor.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student may have multiplied the numerator by 3 instead of 4, confusing the factor needed.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student may have added 5 to the numerator instead of applying multiplicative scaling, revealing an additive misconception.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student may have multiplied by 4.5 or made an arithmetic slip, suggesting the multiplication was attempted but computed incorrectly.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student first write 3 × ? = 12 and then apply the same factor to 2; stretch: write a chain 2/3 = 4/? = 6/? = ?/24.

exercise.description: Fill in blanks with equivalent fractions for 1/7, 2/3, 3/4, 3/5 (more than one answer possible).

items.prompt: Which symbol correctly fills the blank? 5/9 ___ 3/9

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 5/9 > 3/9, because both fractions have the same denominator and 5 > 3.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: When denominators are equal, compare numerators directly: the fraction with the larger numerator is greater.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student may be comparing denominators instead of numerators, or reversing the direction of the symbol.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student may not have noticed the numerators differ, treating 5/9 and 3/9 as the same because denominators match.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student may believe same-denominator fractions cannot be compared without additional steps, indicating the core strategy has not been internalised.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student draw two equal strips each divided into 9 parts and shade 5 and 3 respectively; stretch: write all six fractions with denominator 9 in order from least to greatest.

exercise.description: Compare fractions with same denominator using < and >: 1/4 & 3/4; 3/5 & 4/5; 5/7 & 2/7; 7/8 & 3/8; 5/10 & 6/10; 2/6 & 1/6.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 15. Because 3 × 3 = 9, the denominator must also be multiplied by 3: 5 × 3 = 15.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Identify the factor applied to the numerator (3 → 9 means ×3) and apply the same factor to the denominator.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student draw a chain 3/5 = 6/10 = 9/? by skip-counting numerators and denominators by 3; stretch: find three different equivalent fractions for 3/5 and write them as a chain.

exercise.description: Fill boxes to make equivalent fractions: 2/5 = ?/10; 3/4 = ?/16; 4/7 = 8/?; 5/9 = ?/25.

items.prompt: A worm is 1/3 cm long. Twelve such worms crawl in a line. What is the total length of the line of worms in cm? Use the number line to find your answer.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 4 cm. Each worm is 1/3 cm, and 12 × (1/3) = 12/3 = 4. On the number line, 12 jumps of 1/3 each land at 4.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Count 12 unit-fraction jumps of 1/3 on the number line, or compute 12 × (1/3) = 12/3, then simplify to a whole number.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student mark each 1/3 jump one by one on the number line and count groups of 3 to make wholes; stretch: ask how many worms would make a line of 5 cm.

exercise.description: If an ant is 1/4 cm long, find total length of 16 such ants in a line using the number line.
